ety: Derived from Latin ululāns, present participle of ululō (“to howl”).

s.def: Howling; wailing.

ety: Borrowed from Latin ululō, ululātus, of imitative origin. Cognate with Spanish aullar (“to howl”) and ulular (“to hoot”), and French ululer (“to howl”).

s.def: To howl loudly or prolongedly in lamentation or joy.
ex: Women dance in tight circles, ululating with joy, while groups of men sit nearby watching.

s.def: To produce a rapid and prolonged series of sharp noises with one's voice.

ety: ] Borrowed from Latin ululātiō, from ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”) (from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root) + -ātiō (suffix forming nouns relating to some action or the result of an action) (from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)). By surface analysis, ululate + -ion.

s.def: The act of ululating; a long, loud, wavering cry or howl.
ex: The overthrown Martian set up a prolonged ululation, and immediately a second glittering giant, answering him, appeared over the trees[.]
As ululations and celebratory gunfire filled the air, the mood was one of fragile joy.

ety: From Pitjantjatjara Uluṟu. An old family name, possibly “great pebble” or “Earth mother”.

s.def: A giant free-standing rock in central Australia.

ety: Borrowed from Russian Улья́новск (Ulʹjánovsk), named (1924) after Vladimir Ulyanov, better known as Lenin.

s.def: A city, the administrative center of Ulyanovsk Oblast, Russia, on the Volga river. Birthplace of Vladimir Lenin (born Ulyanov).
An oblast of Russia.

ety: From Japanese 旨味, うまみ (umami), from 旨い (umai, “delicious”) + み (-mi, “-ness”), which describes the quality of a pleasant, savory taste.

s.def: One of the five basic tastes, the savory taste of foods such as seaweed, cured fish, aged cheeses and meats.
ex: But we are, of course, sweaty, fleshy lady-animals – all fur and umami.

ety: Borrowed from Latin umbella (“umbrella”). Compare umbrella, composed of the same etymological elements but formed independently.

s.def: A flat-topped or rounded flower-cluster (= inflorescence) in which the individual flower stalks arise from the same point, the youngest flowers being at the centre.
The pileus of certain fungi.

ety: From Middle French ombre (“umber”), from terre d'ombre (“dark ochre”), from Old French umbre (“shade, shadow”), from Latin umbra. Doublet of umbra.

s.def: A brown clay, somewhat darker than ochre, which contains iron and manganese oxides.
ex: They instructed the upholsterer to do the sofa in cinnamon and the ottoman in umber.
I'll put myself in poor and mean attire, And with a kind of umber smirch my face; The like do you; so shall we pass along, And never stir assailants.

s.def: Alternative form of umbrere.
A grayling.
A dusky brown African wading bird (Scopus umbretta) allied to the shoebill and herons; a hamerkop.
Of a reddish brown colour, like that of the pigment.
ex: Their harps are of the umber shade / That hides the blush of waking day.

s.def: To give a reddish-brown colour to.
ex: Armies o'er armies heap'd, the locusts came, Like clouds in autumn umbering all the sky […]

ety: From Latin umbilicus (“navel”) + -al. By surface analysis, umbilic- + -al.

s.def: Of, or relating to, the navel (umbilicus) or the umbilical cord.
Such that the curvatures of normal sections are all equal to each other.
A cord connecting an astronaut to a spacecraft, or a craft to ground control prior to launch, etc.

ety: From umbilical + cord. Largely displaced native navel-string. First attested in 1753.

The line that supplies an astronaut with oxygen and communications when outside a spacecraft.
Any of the various lines connecting a rocket to its launch pad before liftoff.

An overdependence on or overattachment to support, especially from one's parents or guardians.

ety: Borrowed from Latin umbō (“a shield boss”). Doublet of umbone.

s.def: A boss, or rounded elevation, or a corresponding depression, in a palate, disk, or membrane.

ety: Borrowed from Latin umbra (“shadow”). Doublet of umber.

A shadow.
An uninvited guest brought along by one who was invited.
One of the family Umbridae of mudminnows.
One of genus Umbrina of drums (family Sciaenidae).
An element of the umbral calculus.

ety: From Middle French ombrage (“umbrage”), from Old French ombrage, from Latin umbrāticus (“in the shade”), from umbra (“shadow, shade”).

The president [Mr. Nixon] took umbrage at [The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour's] jokes about him and an unpopular war.

s.def: Shadow; shade.

To shade.

ety: From Middle French ombrageux, or from umbrage + -ous.

s.def: Irritable, easily upset.

ety: Borrowed from Italian ombrella (“parasol, sunshade”), from Late Latin umbrella (influenced by umbra (“shadow, shade”)), from Latin umbella, from umbra + -la (diminutive suffix).

s.def: A cloth-covered frame used for protection against rain or sun.
ex: Quick, grab that umbrella before you get rained on!

s.def: Anything that provides similar protection.

s.def: Anything that provides similar overarching coverage of a range of concepts, purposes, groups, etc.
ex: The test facility was established under the umbrella of the company's quality program.

s.def: A strategy in which five players in the offensive zone form an umbrella-shaped formation around the opposition's goal net.

ex: Jellyfish are composed of more than 90% water and most of their umbrella mass is made up of gelatinous material.

s.def: An umbrella-shaped reflector with a white or silvery inner surface, used to diffuse a nearby light.
ex: Using umbrellas for shooting a wedding party is ok, but not necessary.

s.def: To cover or protect, as if by an umbrella.
ex: Huge pine and eucalyptus umbrellaed the grounds, airconditioning the morning.

s.def: To form the dome shape of an open umbrella.
ex: Bright yellow gowns fit them tightly and umbrellaed from their waist to just below the knees.

s.def: To move like a jellyfish.
ex: The light catches the filigreed tendrils and graceful motion of the jellies, their orange bodies umbrella-ing along like fairy parasols come to life.

s.def: The sedge Cyperus alternifolius.
The palm tree Hedyscepe canterburyana.
A container in which umbrellas are kept when drying or not in use.

ety: From Inuvialuktun ᐅᒥᐊᖅ (umiaq, “women's boat”).

an official who oversees a game or match

ety: From Middle English un-, from Old English un-, from Proto-West Germanic *un-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-. s.def: lack of

ex: un- + loosen → unloosen

s.def: Used to form large numbers as the first in the sequence.

ex: She then untwined the snake from her body, and held it by the tail high above her.

ety: From Middle English *unveilen (suggested by past participle unveiled, vnueylyd (“unveiled”)). Equivalent to un- + veil. To taunt; to reproach; to upbraid.

ety: From up + coming.

ety: From up- + date. Earliest usages from 1940s (see Citations).

How can I update my priors?

ety: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold. Compare Dutch ophouden (“to stop, cease, hold up”), German aufhalten (“to stop, halt, detain”). Compare also Middle Low German upholt, Old Norse upphald (“uphold, support”).

s.def: Ellipsis of palatine uvula, the fleshy appendage that hangs from the back of the soft palate, that closes the nasopharynx during swallowing.
the slight elevation in the mucous membrane immediately behind the internal urethral orifice of the urinary bladder, caused by the middle lobe of the prostate
an object so suspended inside a bell that it may hit the bell and cause it to ring; a clapper

ety: From Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife; overly fond of one’s wife”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives). Uxōrius is derived from uxor (“wife”) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives).

s.def: Of or pertaining to a wife, or her genes or relatives.
Devoted to one's wife; uxorious.
ex: Riccabocca, the wiliest and most relentless of men in his maxims, melted into absolute uxorial imbecility at the sight of that mute distress.

ety: Borrowed from French uxoricide or Latin uxor + English -icide.

s.def: One who murders one's wife.
The murdering of one's own wife.

ety: Borrowed from Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife”), from uxor (“wife”) + -ious.

s.def: Very devoted and possibly submissive to one's wife; showing excessive uxorial devotion.
ex: In truth, Richard was a fond—almost an uxorious husband.
Mr. Watkins Tottle was a rather uncommon compound of strong uxorious inclinations, and an unparalleled degree of anti-connubial timidity.
But Daylight was not unduly uxorious. He lived his man's life just as she lived her woman's life.

ety: From Uyghur ئۇيغۇر (uyghur). Introduced as part of national delimitation in the Soviet Union, reviving the name used by the Uyghur Khaganate. See Uyghurs on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

s.def: A member of a Turkic ethnic group living in northwestern China and southeastern Kazakhstan.
The language of the Uyghur people.
Of, from, or pertaining to the Uyghur people or the Uyghur language.

ety: Borrowed from Uyghur ئۇيغۇرىستان (uyghuristan), from ئۇيغۇر (uyghur) + ـىستان (-istan); by surface analysis, Uyghur + -istan.

s.def: A geographic region of Central Asia, inhabited by Uyghurs.

ety: Etymology tree Chagatai اوزبک (özbäk) Uzbek oʻzbekbor. Russian узбе́к (uzbék)bor. English Uzbek Borrowed from Russian узбе́к (uzbék), borrowed from Uzbek oʻzbek. First attested in 1616. Further etymology is uncertain; possibly from Turkic öz (“genuine”) + Eastern Iranian Sogdian [script needed] (βγ /⁠beġ⁠/, “master”); the latter from Proto-Indo-Aryan *bʰagás, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰagás. The first element is often thought to be equivalent to English Oghuz.

s.def: A member of a Central Asian Turkic ethnic group native to Uzbekistan and neighboring countries, with significant, centuries-old indigenous populations across northern Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan.
Of, from, or pertaining to Uzbekistan, the Uzbek people or the Uzbek language.
ex: He is a gruff, white-bearded man, very Uzbek in his skull-cap and long grey coat.
As for the unpredictable Uzbek commander Dostum, Rasheed said no one knew where he would stand.
Özgön has a university, a brewery and a distinctive bazaar that is very Uzbek in character.

s.def: The language of Uzbekistan.
Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, the name for the Republic of Uzbekistan while under the rule of the Soviet Union (1924-1991).

ety: From Russian Узбекистан (Uzbekistan), itself from Classical Persian اُزْبَکِسْتَان (uzbakistān). Ultimately uncertain; possibly from Turkic uz (“genuine”) + Sogdian [Term?] (/⁠bek⁠/, “master”) (for the second element, see Turkish bey). The suffix is from Classical Persian ـِستان (istān, “place of”). By surface analysis, Uzbek + -i- + -stan.

s.def: A country in Central Asia. Official name: Republic of Uzbekistan. Capital: Tashkent.
ex: Several officers are going to train border police in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, which border Afghanistan, and in several other countries.
She wore a coat made of old cloth from Uzbekistan called a suzani, which was faded black with embroidered red circles and yellow and white zigzags.
In Uzbekistan, forced sterilizations apparently began in 2004 and became official state policy in 2009.

ety: Borrowed from Uyghur ئۈرۈمچى (ürümchi) via its official SASM/GNC/SRC romanization. See there for more.

s.def: A prefecture-level city, the capital of the Xinjiang autonomous region, China.
ex: Before the Wednesday’s suspension, there were 24 flights a week from Kazakhstan to China, including a daily flight to Ürümqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

s.def: A county of Ürümqi city, Xinjiang autonomous region, China.
